detail.longDescription: 🚀 JumpToTech Kubernetes Core Hands-On Lab Objective By the end of this lab, you should understand: Control Plane Worker Nodes Pods Containers Deployment ReplicaSet Self-healing Scaling Labels and selectors StatefulSet Stable Pod identity PersistentVolume (PV) PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) StorageClass Basic Kubernetes troubleshooting PART 1 — Understand Your Kubernetes Cluster Before creating anything, check the cluster. Run: kubectl cluster-info Then: kubectl get nodes Now: kubectl get nodes -o wide Question What are these nodes? Answer Nodes are machines participating in the Kubernetes cluster. Application workloads normally run on Worker Nodes . A simplified architecture looks like this: KUBERNETES CLUSTER CONTROL PLANE ┌─────────────────────┐ │ API Server │ │ Scheduler │ │ Controller Manager │ │ etcd │ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ ───────────┼────────── │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ ↓ ↓ WORKER NODE 1 WORKER NODE 2 ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │ kubelet │ │ kubelet │ │ Pod │ │ Pod │ │ Container │ │ Container │ └────────────┘ └────────────┘ Important components API Server Receives Kubernetes API requests. For example: kubectl get pods and: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml communicate with the Kubernetes API. Scheduler Decides which Worker Node should run a newly created unscheduled Pod. Controller Manager Runs controllers that continuously work to make the actual state match the desired state. etcd Stores Kubernetes cluster state. kubelet Runs on each Worker Node and makes sure assigned Pods are running. PART 2 — Create a Standalone Pod Create a new directory: mkdir kubernetes-core-lab cd kubernetes-core-lab Create: nano pod.yaml Add: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: nginx-pod labels: app: nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.27 ports: - containerPort: 80 Save the file. Apply it: kubectl apply -f pod.yaml Check: kubectl get pods You should see: NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE nginx-pod 1/1 Running 0 ... Now: kubectl get pods -o wide Question What additional information do you see? You should see information including: IP NODE The NODE column tells you which Worker Node is running the Pod. PART 3 — Inspect the Pod Run: kubectl describe pod nginx-pod Find: Node: Labels: Status: IP: Containers: Events: Important kubectl describe is one of the most important troubleshooting commands. When something is wrong, always look at: Events near the bottom. Now check logs: kubectl logs nginx-pod PART 4 — Delete the Standalone Pod Run: kubectl delete pod nginx-pod Check: kubectl get pods Question Did the Pod come back? Answer No. Why? Because we created a standalone Pod . There is no higher-level workload controller responsible for maintaining that Pod. This demonstrates an important production concept: Standalone Pod DELETE POD ↓ Pod disappears ↓ Nothing recreates it This is one reason production applications are normally managed through higher-level workload resources such as Deployments rather than manually creating individual Pods. PART 5 — Create a Deployment Now create: nano deployment.yaml Add: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nginx-deployment spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: nginx template: metadata: labels: app: nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.27 ports: - containerPort: 80 Apply: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml Check: kubectl get deployments Then: kubectl get rs Then: kubectl get pods PART 6 — Understand What Kubernetes Created We created only: Deployment But Kubernetes created: Deployment ↓ ReplicaSet ↓ Pods Run: kubectl get deployment Then: kubectl get rs Then: kubectl get pods Question Did we manually create the ReplicaSet? Answer No. The Deployment created and manages the ReplicaSet. Question Did we manually create the individual Pods? Answer No. The ReplicaSet maintains the required Pod replicas. Conceptually: Deployment │ │ manages ↓ ReplicaSet │ │ maintains ↓ ┌─────────┐ │ Pod # 1 │ ├─────────┤ │ Pod # 2 │ ├─────────┤ │ Pod # 3 │ └─────────┘ PART 7 — Desired State Look inside deployment.yaml : replicas: 3 This tells Kubernetes: DESIRED STATE = 3 Pods Check: kubectl get deployment nginx-deployment You may see something similar to: NAME READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE nginx-deployment 3/3 3 3 Kubernetes continuously tries to make: ACTUAL STATE = DESIRED STATE This process is called reconciliation . PART 8 — Test Kubernetes Self-Healing Get Pods: kubectl get pods Copy one Deployment Pod name. Example: nginx-deployment-7c79c4bf97-abcd1 Delete it: kubectl delete pod nginx-deployment-7c79c4bf97-abcd1 Immediately run: kubectl get pods Better: kubectl get pods -w Watch carefully. You should see a replacement Pod. Press: CTRL+C to stop watching. What happened? Before: Desired = 3 Actual = 3 We deleted one: Desired = 3 Actual = 2 Kubernetes detects the difference. The ReplicaSet works to restore: Desired = 3 Actual = 3 Interview Question Why did the Pod come back? Answer Because the Deployment's ReplicaSet maintains the desired number of replicas. When one Pod disappeared, the ReplicaSet created a replacement. PART 9 — Scale the Deployment Currently: replicas: 3 Scale to 6: kubectl scale deployment nginx-deployment --replicas=6 Check: kubectl get deployment Then: kubectl get pods Question How many Pods? Answer: 6 Now: kubectl get rs The ReplicaSet should show the desired/current replica counts. Now scale down: kubectl scale deployment nginx-deployment --replicas=2 Watch: kubectl get pods -w Kubernetes terminates extra Pods. Stop with: CTRL+C PART 10 — Labels and Selectors Run: kubectl get pods --show-labels You should see labels including: app=nginx Now: kubectl get pods -l app=nginx Why are labels important? Labels allow Kubernetes resources to identify/select other resources. Our Deployment contains: selector: matchLabels: app: nginx and the Pod template contains: labels: app: nginx These must match for this Deployment. Think: Deployment selector ↓ app=nginx ↓ Matching Pods PART 11 — Deployment Update Check the current image: kubectl get deployment nginx-deployment \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}' Now update Nginx: kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deployment \ nginx=nginx:1.28 Watch: kubectl get pods -w Stop with: CTRL+C Check rollout: kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deployment Check history: kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-deployment What happened? Kubernetes performed a rollout. A Deployment allows us to update an application while Kubernetes manages replacement of Pods according to its rollout strategy. PART 12 — Rollback Suppose our new application version has a problem. Rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment Check: kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deployment Then: kubectl get pods Interview Question How do you rollback a Deployment? Answer: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name> PART 13 — Deployment vs StatefulSet Now we move to StatefulSet. Deployment Pods might look like: nginx-deployment-76f8b987d8-x8j2p nginx-deployment-76f8b987d8-82ksa nginx-deployment-76f8b987d8-p91ka The exact generated suffixes can change. StatefulSet Pods look like: web-0 web-1 web-2 StatefulSet gives Pods stable ordinal identities. Concept: DEPLOYMENT Pod A Pod B Pod C Pods are generally interchangeable. Compared with: STATEFULSET web-0 web-1 web-2 Each Pod has a stable identity. PART 14 — Create a StorageClass First check existing StorageClasses: kubectl get storageclass If your cluster already has a default StorageClass, record its name: kubectl get storageclass Example on an AWS EKS cluster might be: gp2 or: gp3 depending on the cluster configuration. Do not blindly create a new StorageClass if your cluster already has the correct one. Set the StorageClass name you actually have: export STORAGE_CLASS=gp2 Replace gp2 if your cluster uses a different StorageClass. Verify: kubectl get storageclass "$STORAGE_CLASS" PART 15 — Create a StatefulSet Create: nano statefulset.yaml Add the following. Replace gp2 with your cluster's StorageClass if necessary. apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nginx-headless spec: clusterIP: None selector: app: nginx-stateful ports: - port: 80 targetPort: 80 --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: StatefulSet metadata: name: nginx-stateful spec: serviceName: nginx-headless replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: nginx-stateful template: metadata: labels: app: nginx-stateful spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.27 ports: - containerPort: 80 volumeMounts: - name: nginx-data mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html volumeClaimTemplates: - metadata: name: nginx-data spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce storageClassName: gp2 resources: requests: storage: 1Gi Apply: kubectl apply -f statefulset.yaml Watch: kubectl get pods -w You should eventually see: nginx-stateful-0 nginx-stateful-1 nginx-stateful-2 PART 16 — Observe StatefulSet Identity Run: kubectl get statefulset Then: kubectl get pods Notice: nginx-stateful-0 nginx-stateful-1 nginx-stateful-2 Compare: DEPLOYMENT nginx-deployment-xxxxx-abc12 nginx-deployment-xxxxx-def34 with: STATEFULSET nginx-stateful-0 nginx-stateful-1 nginx-stateful-2 This stable identity is one of the most important StatefulSet concepts. PART 17 — PVC and PV Run: kubectl get pvc You may see: nginx-data-nginx-stateful-0 nginx-data-nginx-stateful-1 nginx-data-nginx-stateful-2 Check: kubectl get pv Now: kubectl get storageclass Understand the relationship: StatefulSet ↓ nginx-stateful-0 ↓ PVC ↓ PV ↓ Storage PVC PersistentVolumeClaim. The application requests storage. PV PersistentVolume. Represents persistent storage available/bound for Kubernetes use. StorageClass Describes a class of storage and, with dynamic provisioning, tells Kubernetes which provisioner and parameters to use to create storage. PART 18 — Write Data Let's demonstrate why persistent storage matters. Run: kubectl exec nginx-stateful-0 -- \ sh -c 'echo "Hello from JumpToTech StatefulSet" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html' Check: kubectl exec nginx-stateful-0 -- \ cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html Expected: Hello from JumpToTech StatefulSet PART 19 — Delete the StatefulSet Pod Delete: kubectl delete pod nginx-stateful-0 Watch: kubectl get pods -w You should see: nginx-stateful-0 created again. Notice the name. It is still: nginx-stateful-0 not a random new identity. Once it is Running, check the file: kubectl exec nginx-stateful-0 -- \ cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html If storage was correctly provisioned and reattached, you should still see: Hello from JumpToTech StatefulSet This demonstrates two different concepts Stable identity + Persistent storage Do not confuse them. StatefulSet gives the Pod stable identity. PVC/PV provide persistent storage. PART 20 — Compare Deployment and StatefulSet FeatureDeploymentStatefulSetCommon useStateless appsStateful appsPod identityInterchangeable/generatedStable ordinal identityExampleWeb/APIDatabases/clustered stateful systemsTypical namesapp-xxxxx-xxxxxapp-0, app-1ScalingDesigned for interchangeable replicasCan use ordered behaviorStorageCan use persistent storageCommonly paired with per-Pod PVCsRolloutDeployment strategyStatefulSet strategy Important: A StatefulSet does not automatically make a database production-ready . The database itself must still be configured correctly for replication, backups, failover, security, and recovery. PART 21 — BREAK THE APPLICATION Now we intentionally create problems. This is the most important section. A DevOps engineer does not only deploy applications. A DevOps engineer must be able to troubleshoot them. TROUBLESHOOTING LAB 1 — Wrong Image Run: kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deployment \ nginx=nginx:this-image-does-not-exist Wait: kubectl get pods You may see: ErrImagePull followed by: ImagePullBackOff What do you do? First: kubectl describe pod <problem-pod-name> Go to: Events You should find information about the image pull failure. Question Is Kubernetes broken? Answer No. The requested container image/tag cannot be successfully pulled. Fix: kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deployment \ nginx=nginx:1.27 Check: kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deployment TROUBLESHOOTING LAB 2 — CrashLoopBackOff Create: nano broken-pod.yaml Add: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: crash-demo spec: containers: - name: crash image: busybox:1.36 command: - sh - -c - echo "Application starting"; sleep 3; exit 1 Apply: kubectl apply -f broken-pod.yaml Watch: kubectl get pods -w Eventually the container will repeatedly restart and may show: CrashLoopBackOff Stop watching: CTRL+C Now troubleshoot: kubectl describe pod crash-demo Then: kubectl logs crash-demo And: kubectl logs crash-demo --previous Important troubleshooting pattern Something is wrong ↓ kubectl get pods ↓ kubectl describe pod ↓ Check Events ↓ kubectl logs ↓ kubectl logs --previous TROUBLESHOOTING LAB 3 — Pending PVC Do this as a demonstration rather than leaving broken resources in the cluster. Create: nano bad-pvc.yaml Add: apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: broken-pvc spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce storageClassName: storage-class-does-not-exist resources: requests: storage: 1Gi Apply: kubectl apply -f bad-pvc.yaml Check: kubectl get pvc You should see it remain: Pending Investigate: kubectl describe pvc broken-pvc Then: kubectl get storageclass Lesson If you see: Pod Pending and that Pod needs a PVC, check: kubectl get pvc kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> kubectl get storageclass Delete the intentionally broken claim: kubectl delete pvc broken-pvc PART 22 — The Kubernetes Troubleshooting Mindset Do not randomly delete things. Follow a process. Step 1 Check: kubectl get pods Step 2 Get more information: kubectl get pods -o wide Step 3 Describe the problematic resource: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> Step 4 Read: Events Step 5 Check application logs: kubectl logs <pod-name> For a previously crashed container: kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous Step 6 If storage is involved: kubectl get pvc kubectl get pv kubectl get storageclass kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> Step 7 If Deployment is involved: kubectl get deployment kubectl get rs kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> PART 23 — Final Architecture You should now understand this: USER │ │ kubectl apply ↓ API SERVER │ ↓ Desired state stored/processed │ ↓ CONTROLLERS │ ↓ Deployment │ ↓ ReplicaSet │ ↓ Pods │ ↓ SCHEDULER │ │ chooses Node ↓ WORKER NODE │ ↓ kubelet │ ↓ Container Runtime │ ↓ Container Running For a StatefulSet: StatefulSet │ ├── nginx-stateful-0 │ │ │ └── PVC → PV → Storage │ ├── nginx-stateful-1 │ │ │ └── PVC → PV → Storage │ └── nginx-stateful-2 │ └── PVC → PV → Storage PART 24 — Student Challenge Do this section without instructor help. Challenge 1 Create a Deployment named: student-web Requirements: Image: nginx:1.27 Replicas: 4 Label: app=student-web Container port: 80 Verify: kubectl get deployment kubectl get rs kubectl get pods Challenge 2 Delete one Pod. Prove Kubernetes recreates it. Challenge 3 Scale: 4 → 7 Then: 7 → 2 Challenge 4 Update Nginx to: nginx:1.28 Watch the rollout. Challenge 5 Break the image intentionally. Use: nginx:does-not-exist Troubleshoot it. Then repair it. Challenge 6 Explain: Deployment ↓ ReplicaSet ↓ Pod ↓ Container Challenge 7 Explain the difference between: Deployment and: StatefulSet without looking at your notes. FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS 1. What is a Pod? A Pod is Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit and contains one or more containers. 2. What is a Deployment? A Deployment manages stateless application workloads and declaratively manages ReplicaSets and application updates. 3. What is a ReplicaSet? A ReplicaSet maintains the desired number of matching Pod replicas. 4. What happens when a Deployment Pod dies? Its ReplicaSet works to create a replacement so the desired replica count is restored. 5. What is StatefulSet? A workload controller designed for applications that need stable Pod identities and often stable per-Pod storage. 6. Deployment vs StatefulSet? Deployment replicas are generally interchangeable. StatefulSet Pods have stable ordinal identities such as: mysql-0 mysql-1 mysql-2 7. What does Scheduler do? It chooses an appropriate Node for an unscheduled Pod. 8. What does kubelet do? It runs on each Worker Node and works with the container runtime to ensure assigned Pods are running. 9. What does API Server do? It exposes the Kubernetes API and is the central entry point for API operations. 10. What is etcd? It is the distributed key-value store used by Kubernetes to store cluster state. 11. What is PV? PersistentVolume — a Kubernetes resource representing persistent storage. 12. What is PVC? PersistentVolumeClaim — a request for persistent storage. 13. What does PVC Bound mean? The claim has been successfully bound to a PersistentVolume. 14. What does Pending mean? The resource cannot yet proceed to its required running/bound state. You need to investigate why. 15. What is ImagePullBackOff ? Kubernetes cannot successfully pull the requested container image and is backing off between retry attempts. 16. What is CrashLoopBackOff ? A container repeatedly starts, fails, and Kubernetes delays subsequent restart attempts. 17. First command when a Pod has a problem? Start with: kubectl get pods Then investigate: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> and: kubectl logs <pod-name> 18. Where do you look in kubectl describe ? Especially: Events 19. How do you see which Node runs a Pod? kubectl get pods -o wide 20. Explain what happens after kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml . A strong answer: kubectl sends an API request to the Kubernetes API Server. The requested desired state is persisted in the cluster. The Deployment controller observes the Deployment and manages the appropriate ReplicaSet. The ReplicaSet works to create the required Pods. The Scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to suitable Nodes. The kubelet on each selected Worker Node observes the assigned Pod and works with the container runtime to start the required containers. Kubernetes controllers continuously reconcile actual state with desired state. CLEANUP Delete the lab resources: kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml kubectl delete -f statefulset.yaml kubectl delete -f broken-pod.yaml kubectl delete pod nginx-pod --ignore-not-found kubectl delete pvc broken-pvc --ignore-not-found kubectl delete deployment student-web --ignore-not-found Check: kubectl get pods kubectl get deployment kubectl get statefulset kubectl get pvc What You Must Remember CONTROL PLANE ↓ Manages the cluster WORKER NODE ↓ Runs workloads POD ↓ Runs container(s) DEPLOYMENT ↓ Manages ReplicaSets and stateless application rollout REPLICASET ↓ Maintains Pod replicas STATEFULSET ↓ Stable Pod identity PVC ↓ Requests storage PV ↓ Represents persistent storage And the most important Kubernetes idea: DESIRED STATE ↓ Kubernetes checks ↓ ACTUAL STATE ↓ Something is wrong? ↓ RECONCILIATION ↓ Move actual state toward the desired state # devops # infrastructure # kubernetes # software # coding # development # engineering # inclusive # community Pods Deployments ReplicaSets StatefulSets Storage Troubleshooting
